title: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn
summary:
Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.
Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.
"It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said.
The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment.
Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments.

title: A New Ice Age Was Beginning. Then Humans Started Burning Fossil Fuels
summary:
Burning fossil fuels may have stopped the Earth from entering another ice age, a new study suggests.
The findings shows the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers parts of Canada’s Baffin Island, started growing a few thousand years ago before rapidly reversing course beginning in the 1960s as carbon pollution ramped up.
It retreated to form the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers an area the size of Delaware on Baffin Island.
Unlike glaciers, which can move, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the bedrock, preserving the vegetal record of what grew around it under the ice.

title: Streeting: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies
summary:
Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.
Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".
Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime".
Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".
"It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time.

title: Brutal summer heat killed more than 50,000 in Europe’s cities
summary:
More than 50,000 people are estimated to have died across Europe’s cities during the brutal heat waves that roiled the continent this summer — making this year’s heat the region’s deadliest on record, according to a new analysis.
Europe is the fastest-warming continent and extreme heat, the deadliest form of extreme weather, is already becoming unbearable.
Sign up for the newsletterThey estimated a total of 50,391 heat-related deaths across the cities, which make up about 40% of the population of the countries studied.
The scientists also found the role of climate change in heat deaths is becoming more pronounced.
Earlier this century, fossil fuel pollution was responsible for about 40% of heat deaths compared to around two-thirds today.

title: Denmark nurdles may be from River Tyne spill, says Danish environment agency
summary:
Nurdles found along the Danish coast are likely to originate from the spill in north-east England, according to the country's environment agency.
Masses of plastic pellets were found along the western coast of Denmark in September.
The Danish Environment Protection Agency has now confirmed tests carried out on the microplastics suggest they originated from the River Tyne spill in July.
Signe Simonsen, the head of startup Race for Oceans Technology, first spotted the nurdles on the island of Mandø in Denmark on 26 September.
"There were just so many milk white plastic pellets," she said.

title: Greetings from the Brazil-Argentina border, where waterfalls are flowing at near-record rates
summary:
Greetings from the Brazil-Argentina border, where waterfalls are flowing at near-record ratesCarrie Kahn/NPRIGUAZÚ NATIONAL PARK, Argentina — Few times in my life have I felt the enormity and power of nature.
Standing at the edge of Iguazú Falls, on the Brazil-Argentina border, was one of them.
A rain-soaked October in Brazil has sent near-record volumes of water surging over its towering cliffs.
But what a spectacular force of nature for the lower-than-average number of tourists who braved the deluge this month.
The roar of the rushing Iguazú river under your feet penetrates your body; your eyes strain to keep up as the rusty swells disappear over the steep precipice.

title: Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
summary:
Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebelstoggle caption i Abdulnasser Alseddik/APDrinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.
The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies.
As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.
Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop.
Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city.
